newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan finance firms shuffle off loan shark image.
newsitem.headline: Japan finance firms shuffle off loan shark image.

text.p: Japan's consumer finance firms, once regarded as loan sharks living off the misfortunes of the cash-strapped, have spiffed up their image and clientele, and the profits are rolling in.

"Consumer finance industry leaders have conquered their negative image by going public, which is helping reel in customers," said Shuji Kaminaka of Okasan Economic Research Institute. "The installation of automated lending machines and tie-ups with banks have also made it easier to borrow money."
The latest of the firms to debut on the Tokyo stock market is Japan's biggest, Takefuji Corp, listed on Friday.

In the business year that ended on March 31, Takefuji posted a parent current profit of 110.77 billion yen ($1.02 billion), which is seen jumping to 125.50 billion yen ($1.16 billion) this year, Nomura Research Institute said.
Industry sources say the firms have secure foundations, as they are not burdened by non-performing loans to corporations.
"Irrecoverable loans stand at about 40,000 cases per firm per year," Kaminaka said. "But since loans are in small lots averaging about 400,000 yen ($3,703), it is not a burden."

Ultra-low interest rates are also encouraging for the finance firms, which in the past have been criticised for outrageous rates and hard-nosed collecting methods. Japan's current historically low market rates are a boon to the firms, who raise funds by borrowing from other financial institutions.
Now, most of the major firms' rates are set between 25 and 28 percent per annum, a Takefuji spokesman said. Takefuji's record-high rate, some 10 years ago, was 41 percent, he said.
Analysts say the key to growth is increasing market share.

Shops with counter clerks are being replaced by unmanned dispensing machines strategically placed near train stations. These are attracting more and more people in their 20s and 30s short of petty cash, as well as the financially woebegone.

Acom Co Ltd is the second-biggest in the industry, but analysts see only limited scope for it to grow. UBS said its parent current profit are expected to rise slightly to 79.2 billion yen ($733 million) in the business year to next March.
"Acom has the smallest possibility for expansion, as it was the first to use automated lending machines," said UBS Securities analyst Ayako Sato.

Analysts said Promise Co Ltd, ranking third, had the largest potential because it was the newcomer in the area of automatic lending machines. Daiwa Institute of Research said Promise would post 72 billion yen ($666 million) in profits in 1996/97 against 60.8 billion yen ($562 million) last year.
"The number of (Promise's) new customers rose 33 percent year-on-year in April-June due to an increase in loan machine numbers and extended business hours," a Daiwa analyst said.
Analysts said Takefuji's growth was likely to tread water.

"There is not much room for expansion," a Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics analyst said. "But Takefuji is the top firm in the industry and has a major chunk of the business, so other firms will buckle before it does."
In the Tokyo's stock market, brokers said debutant Takefuji, immensely popular since its auction, would reign.
"If a fund manager wanted a consumer financer in his portfolio, he would probably want the industry leader and would give up other financers' shares to include it," a broker said.
Market sources said Sanyo Shinpan Finance Co Ltd could be a prime candidate for replacement in fund managers' portfolios.

"Most of its business is in southern Japan," an analyst at a "Big Four" brokerage said. "There is not much chance for it to expand into larger cities like Tokyo or Osaka because the three largest firms have most of the market share." ($1=108)
